name: Injection and XSS
intent: Stop untrusted input from being treated as code: keep data and commands separate in database queries, and encode output so the browser shows user text instead of running it.
scenario: A shop has a login form that looks up a user by name, and a product page that shows customer reviews. Anyone on the internet can type anything into both.
problem: Many of the most damaging attacks work the same way: the application builds a command by pasting user input into it, and the receiver cannot tell where the programmer's text ends and the attacker's begins. In a database this is SQL injection, in a web page it is cross-site scripting (XSS), and the same shape appears in shell commands, LDAP and templates.

howItWorks.title: How SQL injection happens
howItWorks.text: If the code builds a query by joining strings, such as "... WHERE name = '" + name + "'", then input containing a quote character can end the value early and add its own conditions or commands. Typing a value like  ' OR '1'='1  can turn a lookup for one user into 'every user'.

howItWorks.title: Fix it with parameterized queries
howItWorks.text: Send the query text with placeholders and the values separately. The database compiles the query first, and the values are only ever data, whatever characters they contain. Object-relational mappers do this by default, but raw string building inside them reopens the hole.

howItWorks.title: How XSS happens
howItWorks.text: If the page inserts user-supplied text into HTML unchanged, input such as a script tag or an event attribute becomes part of the page and runs in every visitor's browser, with their cookies and session. The attacker can then act as that user.

howItWorks.title: Fix it by encoding output for where it lands
howItWorks.text: Escape special characters when writing user data into HTML (< becomes <), and use the right encoding for attributes, URLs and JavaScript contexts. Modern frameworks escape by default; the dangerous calls are the ones with names like innerHTML, dangerouslySetInnerHTML or 'raw'.

howItWorks.title: Add layers
howItWorks.text: Validate input against what is expected (type, length, allowed characters) as a first filter, not as the only defence. Give the database account minimal rights so an injection cannot drop tables. Send a Content-Security-Policy header to limit which scripts may run, and mark session cookies HttpOnly so scripts cannot read them.

pros: Parameterized queries and output encoding remove whole classes of attack, not individual payloads
Standard, cheap and supported by every mainstream framework
Defence in depth (least privilege, CSP, HttpOnly cookies) limits the damage of a missed spot
Fixing it at the boundary protects every future input
cons: One forgotten concatenation or raw HTML call is enough to be vulnerable
Blocklists of bad characters are easy to bypass and break legitimate input
Encoding must match the context, which developers often get wrong
Dynamic parts such as table or column names cannot be parameters and need an allow-list
whenToUse: Always: every query and every page that includes data from outside your control
Treat data from users, other services, files and even your own database as untrusted when building queries or output
whenNotToUse: Never rely on input filtering alone, or on escaping quotes by hand, in place of parameters
Never turn encoding off to 'fix' a display problem
pitfalls: Building SQL with string concatenation or interpolation, even 'just for sorting'
Using innerHTML or raw template output for user content
Sanitizing on input instead of encoding on output, so the data is wrong in other contexts
Running the application's database user with admin rights

roles.label: User or attacker
roles.description: Supplies input that must be treated as data.

roles.label: Application
roles.description: Builds queries and pages from that input.

roles.label: Database or browser
roles.description: Interprets what the application sends it.

quiz.question: A login handler builds the query by joining the typed username into the SQL text. Someone enters ' OR '1'='1 and is logged in as the first user. Which change best removes the root cause?
options: Escape single quotes and backslashes in the username by hand before building the query
Use a parameterized query, so the username is sent as data apart from the SQL text, never parsed
Reject usernames that contain the words OR or SELECT
Limit usernames to 30 characters so long attack strings cannot fit
quiz.explanation: With parameters the database never parses the value as SQL, whatever characters it holds. Hand escaping and word lists are bypassed with other tricks, and a length limit does not stop short payloads like this one.

quiz.question: A product page prints customer reviews into the HTML. An attacker posts a review that contains a script tag, and it runs in every visitor's browser. Which change fixes the root cause?
options: Remove the string script from reviews when they are submitted, and store the cleaned text
Mark the session cookie HttpOnly, so the injected script can no longer cause any harm
Encode review text for the HTML context when writing the page, so it is shown as text
Send a Content-Security-Policy header and leave the page code unchanged
quiz.explanation: Output encoding turns the markup into inert text where it lands. Blocklists on input are easy to bypass, and HttpOnly and CSP only limit the damage, they do not remove the injection.

quiz.question: An orders endpoint uses parameterized queries everywhere. The sort option comes from the URL, as in ?sort=created_at, and is added to the SQL as ORDER BY followed by the value. A developer proposes passing it as a bound parameter instead. What is the best approach?
options: Map the value to a fixed allow-list of column names, as identifiers cannot be bound
Bind it as a parameter, because placeholders work for any part of the statement
Escape quotes in the value, check that it is shorter than 20 characters and then add it
Strip all characters except letters and underscores, then insert it into the query
quiz.explanation: A bound parameter becomes a literal value, not an identifier, so it cannot name a column. Only values from a fixed list should ever reach the SQL text. Character stripping is a weaker filter that still lets any column or SQL keyword through.
